Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Units 728/730 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Units (WMU) 728 and 730 are located in east central Alberta within the Red Deer North 
Saskatchewan Region. The Units are approximately 612 km2 and defined by the boundaries of the Canadian 
Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright. WMU 728 is contained within the east portion of WMU 232 while WMU 730 is 
within the west portion of WMU 234. Highway 41 runs north-south and separates the two WMU’s. The land is 
owned and operated by Canadian National Defence and is an active military training facility. 
 
The most recent previous aerial ungulate survey conducted in this unit used the transect survey method and was 
conducted in 2019. Results of previous surveys are summarized in Tables 1-3. 
 
The objective of the survey conducted in February 2020 was to assess the status of the ungulate population in this 
WMU by determining estimates of population size, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of interest, including carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or species at risk. 
 
Survey Method 
 
From February 24-25, 2020, a strip transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) 
intervals for 25% coverage (with 400 m wide survey strip) for a total survey effort of 150 km2 (376 linear kms flown). 
Snow conditions were good and uniformly consistent throughout the unit. At each observation point, moose were 
counted, and, when possible, classified by sex and age. Sex and age classification was determined for moose by 
identification of vulva patch and size differential of cow/calves. Due to time of year and antler drop, deer were 
classified by species and not age or sex. 
 
Density was calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in Krebs 
2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the transect lengths varied. 
Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were also 
calculated. A correction factor of 83% for deer detectability was applied to population and density estimates (Habib 
et al. 2012), with a factor of 95% applied to moose density and population estimates. 
 
Elk observations were recorded during the survey, but population estimates were not calculated because the 
design of this survey is not appropriate for elk population calculation. 
 
Results 
There were 437 white-tailed deer observed in 112 groups. The average white-tailed deer density was estimated at 
3.40 individuals/km2. Population was estimated at 2082 (Table 1). 
 
There were 538 mule deer observed within 90 groups. The average mule deer density was estimated at 4.18 
individuals/km2. Population was estimated at 2563 (Table 2). 
 
There were 135 moose observed within 72 groups. Of the 135 moose identified, 52 (37%) were bulls, 55 (40%) 
were cows, 32 (23%) were calves and 0 (0%) were not classified. The bull:cow ratio was 0.95 and the calf:cow 
ratio was 0.58 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated at 0.94 individuals/km2. Population was 
estimated at 577 (Table 3); 216 bulls, 228 cows and 133 calves. 
Lastly, there were 410 elk (both on and off transect) observed within 23 groups. 
We also observed 48 coyotes, and 19 sharp-tailed grouse. These are incidental observations only and should not 
be considered minimum total counts.
